author: Epiphanius of Salamis
occasion: A eucharistic prayer attributed to Epiphanius, giving thanks for God's benefits and recounting the institution of the Lord's Supper, with a petition for the transformation of the bread and cup.
argument: The prayer first thanks God for sending his eternal Son, the divine Word, who became fully human without ceasing to be God, one Christ, one Lord in deity and humanity, without confusion and without division. It then recounts how Christ, before his voluntary death, took bread, gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples as his body, and likewise the cup mixed from two elements, from the fruit of the vine and water, as his blood of the new covenant for the forgiveness of sins. Finally it asks that the bread and the cup may become the body and blood of Christ, saving for souls and bodies, so that the faithful may share in the holy mysteries in newness of spirit.

outline.move: Thanksgiving to God for sending his eternal Son, the Word, who became fully human without change or division, one Christ, one Lord in deity and humanity.
Recital of Christ's institution of the Eucharist: the bread as his body and the cup mixed from wine and water as his blood of the new covenant for forgiveness of sins.
Petition that the bread and cup may become the body and blood of Christ, saving for souls and bodies, for participation in the holy mysteries.

cast.name: God
cast.who: God the Father, to whom the prayer of thanksgiving is addressed.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The eternal Son and Word of God, who became human and instituted the Eucharist.

cast.name: The disciples
cast.who: The holy disciples, his holy apostles, to whom Christ gave the bread and cup.

voices.speaker: Christ
voices.how_marked: Introduced by εἰπών ('saying') and marked by direct quotation, with two separate sayings, one for the bread and one for the cup, each introduced by εἰπών.

key_terms.sense: The divine Word, the eternal Son of God who became flesh.
Sharing the throne of God's kingdom, indicating the Son's co-equal divine rule.
Co-eternal with the Father, without beginning.
Human nature, which the Word took on fully.
The union of deity and humanity in Christ without confusion and without separation.
Divine signs or miracles that attest Christ's divine nature.
Christ's death as voluntary, freely chosen.
Life-giving, describing Christ's death as the source of life.
Forgiveness of sins, the purpose of Christ's body and blood being given.
The new covenant established by Christ's blood.
The cup as a cup of immortality, conveying eternal life.
The change or transformation of the bread into Christ's body.
The holy mysteries, the eucharistic elements and the sacred rite.
Newness of spirit, contrasted with the oldness of the letter, indicating spiritual renewal.

scripture: The text alludes to the Last Supper accounts (Matthew 26:26-28; Mark 14:22-24; Luke 22:19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-25) and to the Word becoming flesh (John 1:14). The author uses Greek biblical language; modern citations should follow standard English Bible references (e.g., Matthew, Mark, Luke, 1 Corinthians, John).
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; the attribution to Epiphanius of Salamis is traditional but not definitively established.
The original liturgical context and whether this anaphora was actually used in worship is uncertain.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μὴ ὑπομείνας τροπήν... οὐκ ἀλλοιώσας τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα, οὐχὶ δύο ὑπάρχων, ἀλλ' εἷς βασιλεύς, εἷς Χριστός, εἷς Κύριος θεότητι καὶ ἀνθρωπότητι, ἀφύρτως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως
_unresolved_facts.fix: The prayer emphasizes that the Word became flesh without undergoing change (τροπήν), without altering humanity, not existing as two but as one King, one Christ, one Lord in deity and humanity, without confusion and without division. The text does not explicitly state 'without ceasing to be God.'

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: σὰρξ καὶ ψυχὴν ἔννουν ἀνθρώπου ἔχων καὶ πάντα τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
_unresolved_facts.fix: having flesh and ensouled soul of a human and all that belongs to a human without sin

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι ἐπὶ τὸν ἑκούσιον καὶ ἀοίδιμον καὶ ζωοποιὸν τὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν θάνατον
_unresolved_facts.fix: about to come to the voluntary, glorious, and life-giving death on our behalf
having given thanks, having blessed, having sanctified, he gave

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: σῶμα σωτήριον ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων... αἷμα σωτήριόν ἐστιν ἡμῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: body saving of souls and bodies... blood saving for us

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μὴ ὑπομείνας τροπήν... ἀφύρτως καὶ ἀδιαιρέτως
_unresolved_facts.fix: without undergoing change, without confusion and without division

_unresolved_facts.claim: two separate sayings, one for the bread and one for the cup, each introduced by εἰπών
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀποστόλοις εἰπών· Λάβετε, φάγετε... Ὡσαύτως μετὰ τὸ δειπνῆσαι, λαβὼν ποτήριον... ἔδωκε τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ εἰπών· Πίετε ἐξ αὐτοῦ πάντες
_unresolved_facts.fix: Two separate sayings, but the first is introduced by εἰπών with dative ἀποστόλοις, while the second is introduced by εἰπών with dative τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ. The first saying is introduced after 'holy apostles,' the second after 'his disciples.'

_unresolved_facts.fix: God the Father, to whom the prayer is addressed and to whom Christ showed the bread
